label: Institution
name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church – Alternative synod
summary:
The Bulgarian Orthodox Church Alternative Synod (also known as the Bulgarian Orthodox Church in Schism, or the Pimen Schism after its patriarch Pimen), which existed from 1992 to 2004, was a schismatic Bulgarian Orthodox body that rejected the post-communist Bulgarian Orthodox Church's leadership under Patriarch Maxim (elected 1971 under communist oversight) as illegitimate — a dispute that reflected the broader post-1989 struggle in Eastern Europe over churches' communist-era institutional legacies and their claims to authentic Orthodox identity.

Patriarch Maxim had been elected in 1971 through a process controlled by the communist state security services (according to declassified files), and a significant portion of the Bulgarian Orthodox clergy and laity viewed his leadership as tainted by collaboration. After communism's fall (1989-1990), a reform movement within the Bulgarian church pressed for Maxim's resignation; when he refused, the reformers convened an alternative synod in 1992 and elected Metropolitan Pimen as rival patriarch, triggering a schism that divided Bulgarian Orthodoxy for over a decade.

The dispute became entangled in Bulgarian politics — the UDF (anti-communist opposition) tended to support the Alternative Synod, while the BSP (ex-communist) government supported Patriarch Maxim. Physical confrontations occurred at Orthodox churches as each side tried to take control of buildings. The schism ended in 2004 when the Council of European Churches and the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople facilitated reconciliation, and all bishops of the Alternative Synod were received back into canonical unity under Patriarch Maxim.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Bulgarian Orthodox Church Alternative Synod — a 12-year schism reflecting post-communist Bulgaria's struggle with the institutional legacy of communist-controlled religion, resolved through pan-Orthodox mediation — is a significant case study in post-communist religious de-legitimation and reconciliation.
